fields.title: Tell Me the Story – Book 2: Out of Egypt
fields.subtitle: Old Testament Stories from Exodus to Ruth
fields.description: Twenty-one Bible stories from Exodus to Ruth for children aged 6 to 10, each short enough to read aloud at bedtime: the baby in the basket, the burning bush, the Passover, the path through the sea, bread from heaven, the walls of Jericho, Deborah, Gideon's three hundred, and Ruth and Boaz. Every story ends with a prayer and three questions to talk about together. The second book of Tell Me the Story.
fields.about_html:
Tell Me the Story is an original Ochorus storybook Bible for children aged 6 to 10, in eight books and three parts: Old Testament Stories, The Life of Jesus, and New Testament Stories. God is the hero of every story, and the whole Bible is one story that leads to Jesus.

Book 2, “Out of Egypt”, tells twenty-one stories from Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges and Ruth: how God rescued His people from slavery, fed them in the desert, gave them His commandments and brought them into the promised land. It meets brave women like Rahab, Deborah and Ruth, and ends with the birth of King David’s grandfather. Where the New Testament itself links a story to Jesus, as John 3:14 does with the bronze snake, a line says so.

The stories stay close to what the Bible says, and the people in them say what the Bible says they said, in simple words. Hard stories, like the Passover night, the golden calf, Jericho and Samson, are told honestly but gently. Each takes about four minutes to read aloud, and under each are three questions to talk about together, with answers for the grown-up reading along. Book 1 is not required.

qa.question: Which stories are in Book 2 of Tell Me the Story?
qa.answer: Twenty-one stories from Exodus to Ruth: baby Moses, the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover, the path through the sea, manna, Moses' tired arms, the Ten Commandments, the golden calf, the tabernacle, the twelve spies, the bronze snake, Balaam's donkey, Rahab, crossing the Jordan, Jericho, Deborah, Gideon, Samson, and two stories of Ruth.

qa.question: Do I need to read Book 1 first?
qa.answer: No. Each book stands on its own. Book 2 begins with a short introduction that picks up the story from Joseph's family in Egypt.

qa.question: How are hard stories like the Passover and Jericho told?
qa.answer: Honestly but gently. The Passover night, Jericho and Samson's death are each told in a sentence or two without frightening detail, and the questions help a grown-up talk them through.

qa.question: How does it point to Jesus?
qa.answer: Where the New Testament itself links a story to Jesus, a short "Looking ahead to Jesus" line says so: the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), the manna (John 6:35), the rock (1 Corinthians 10:4), the tabernacle (John 1:14), the bronze snake (John 3:14), and Rahab and Ruth in Jesus' family tree (Matthew 1:5).

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every verse quoted with its reference is word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), which is in the public domain.

qa.question: Can it be read aloud at bedtime?
qa.answer: Yes, that is what it is written for. Each story takes about four minutes to read aloud, and each chapter has a Listen button that reads it at a gentle speed and then asks the three questions.

fields.title: Introduction: The God Who Rescues
fields.body_html:
“The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” — Exodus 15:2

At the end of the last book, Joseph’s whole family went to live in Egypt, where there was food in the famine. Jacob’s twelve sons had children, and their children had children, until there were thousands and thousands of them. They were called the Israelites, because Jacob’s other name was Israel.

But this book begins with a problem. A new king came to rule Egypt, and he made the Israelites into slaves.

Had God forgotten His promises to Abraham? Had He forgotten that He would give Abraham’s family a land of their own, and bless the whole world through them?

No. God never forgets His promises. This is the book where God rescues His people. You will meet a baby in a basket, a bush that burns without burning up, and a sea that opens like a door. You will see bread fall from the sky and water pour out of a rock, and walls come tumbling down. You will meet brave women like Rahab and Deborah and Ruth, and a not-very-brave man called Gideon whom God made brave.

You will also see God’s people grumbling and complaining and disobeying, again and again. And you will see God being patient with them, again and again.

The Bible tells this story so that we can know what God is like. He hears His people when they cry. He keeps His promises. And He is the God who rescues.

Dear God, thank you that you hear people when they cry out to you. As we read these stories, help us to trust you, the God who rescues. Amen.

study_questions.question: What happened to Jacob’s family in Egypt at the start of this book?
study_questions.answer: There were thousands of them by now, called the Israelites, and a new king of Egypt made them into slaves.

study_questions.question: What is this book mostly about?
study_questions.answer: How God rescued His people from Egypt and led them towards the land He had promised Abraham.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that God is “the God who rescues”?
study_questions.answer: He saves people who can’t save themselves. He rescued Israel from Egypt, and in the end He sent Jesus to rescue us from sin.

fields.title: A Baby in a Basket
fields.body_html:
“She named him Moses and explained, ‘I drew him out of the water.’” — Exodus 2:10

A new king came to rule Egypt. The kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh. This Pharaoh had never known Joseph, and he didn’t care what Joseph had done to save Egypt long ago.

Pharaoh looked at the Israelites and was afraid. “There are too many of them,” he said. “If war comes, they might join our enemies.” So he made them slaves. He put cruel slave drivers over them and made them build whole cities for him, with bricks and mortar, in the hot sun.

But the harder the Egyptians made them work, the more the Israelites grew.

So Pharaoh made a terrible plan. He told the Hebrew midwives, the women who helped mothers when their babies were born, to kill every baby boy. But the midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, loved God more than they feared Pharaoh. They let the boys live. And God was kind to the midwives.

Then Pharaoh gave an even more terrible order to all his people: “Every Hebrew baby boy must be thrown into the River Nile.”

At that time, an Israelite woman had a baby boy. He was a beautiful baby, and she hid him for three months. But babies grow, and they cry, and soon she couldn’t hide him any longer.

So she made a little basket out of papyrus reeds and coated it with tar, so the water couldn’t get in. She laid her baby in the basket and set it among the tall reeds at the edge of the river. His big sister stood a little way off to see what would happen.

Then Pharaoh’s own daughter came down to the river to bathe. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant girl to fetch it. When she opened it, there was the baby, crying! She felt so sorry for him. “This is one of the Hebrew babies,” she said.

His sister was ready. She stepped forward and said, “Shall I go and find one of the Hebrew women to feed the baby for you?”

“Yes, go,” said Pharaoh’s daughter.

And who do you think the girl fetched? The baby’s own mother! Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this baby and feed him for me, and I will pay you.” So the baby’s mother got to take her own son home, and look after him, and she was even paid for it!

When the boy was older, his mother took him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, which sounds like the Hebrew words for “drawn out”, because she said, “I drew him out of the water.”

Pharaoh wanted to destroy God’s people. But God used Pharaoh’s own daughter to save the very boy who would one day lead them all to freedom.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 1–2:10

Dear God, thank you that you watch over little babies and children. Thank you that no one can stop your plans. Help me to be brave like Shiphrah and Puah and Moses’ sister. Amen.

study_questions.question: How did Moses’ mother keep him safe from Pharaoh?
study_questions.answer: She hid him for three months, then made a waterproof basket and set him among the reeds at the edge of the river while his sister watched.

study_questions.question: Who found the baby, and what surprising thing happened next?
study_questions.answer: Pharaoh’s own daughter found him. Then Moses’ sister fetched his real mother, who was paid to look after her own baby.

study_questions.question: The midwives and Moses’ sister were brave. When might you need to be brave to do what is right?
study_questions.answer: Perhaps when others want you to join in with something unkind, or when it’s scary to speak up. Like the midwives, we can trust God more than we fear people.

fields.title: The Bush That Didn’t Burn Up
fields.body_html:
“God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM.’” — Exodus 3:14

Moses grew up in Pharaoh’s palace, but he knew he was an Israelite. One day, when he was grown up, he saw an Egyptian beating one of his people, and Moses killed the Egyptian. When Pharaoh heard about it, he wanted to kill Moses. So Moses ran away, far into the desert, to a land called Midian.

There Moses married a woman named Zipporah, and he became a shepherd. For forty years he looked after his father-in-law’s sheep in the wilderness. He must have thought he would never see Egypt again.

But God had not forgotten the Israelites. They groaned under their heavy work, and they cried out for help. And God heard them. God remembered His promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

One day Moses led the sheep to the far side of the desert, to Horeb, the mountain of God. And there he saw something very strange. A bush was on fire, but it didn’t burn up! The flames kept on burning, but the leaves and branches stayed just as they were.

“I must go over and see this,” said Moses.

When God saw him coming, He called to him from the middle of the bush. “Moses! Moses!”

“Here I am,” said Moses.

“Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.”

Moses took off his sandals and hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.

“I have seen how my people are suffering in Egypt,” said God. “I have heard them crying out, and I know how much they are hurting. I have come down to rescue them, and to bring them to a good land, a land flowing with milk and honey. So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people out of Egypt.”

But Moses said, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?”

“I will be with you,” said God.

“But what if the people ask me what Your name is?” said Moses. “What shall I tell them?”

God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. Tell them, ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God’s name means that He has always been, and always will be. Nobody made Him, and nobody can stop Him.

Moses still had excuses. “What if they don’t believe me?” So God gave him signs. When Moses threw his shepherd’s staff on the ground, it turned into a snake! When he picked it up by the tail, it turned back into a staff.

“But I’m not good at speaking,” said Moses.

“Who made people’s mouths?” said God. “Isn’t it I, the Lord? Now go. I will help you speak.”

But Moses said, “Please, Lord, send someone else.”

God was angry with Moses. But He was still patient with him. He said that Moses’ brother Aaron would go with him and help him speak.

So Moses picked up his staff, and set off back to Egypt.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Many years later, Jesus said, “Before Abraham was born, I am!” (John 8:58). Jesus was using God’s own name from the burning bush. He was saying that He is God.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 3–4

Dear God, thank you that you see people who are suffering and hear them when they cry. When I feel too small for what you want me to do, help me remember that you are with me. Amen.

study_questions.question: What was strange about the bush Moses saw?
study_questions.answer: It was on fire, but it didn’t burn up.

study_questions.question: What did God tell Moses His name was, and what does it mean?
study_questions.answer: “I AM WHO I AM.” It means God has always been and always will be. Nobody made Him and nobody can stop Him.

study_questions.question: Moses made lots of excuses. What was God’s answer to “Who am I?”
study_questions.answer: “I will be with you.” What matters most isn’t how strong or clever we are, but that God is with us.

fields.title: “Let My People Go!”
fields.body_html:
“This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go.’” — Exodus 5:1

Moses and his brother Aaron went to the palace and stood in front of the king of Egypt. Moses was eighty years old by now.

“This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says,” they told him. “‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness.’”

Pharaoh just laughed at them. “Who is the Lord, that I should obey Him?” he said. “I don’t know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go!”

And Pharaoh made things even worse. “Those lazy Israelites!” he said. “Stop giving them straw to make bricks. Let them go and find their own straw. But they must still make just as many bricks as before.”

Now the Israelites had to run all over Egypt looking for straw, and they still had to make all those bricks. When they couldn’t, the slave drivers beat them. The Israelites were angry with Moses. “You’ve only made things worse!” they said.

Moses went to God. “Why have you brought trouble on these people?” he asked. “You haven’t rescued them at all!”

“Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh,” God said. “I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the heavy work of the Egyptians. I will take you as my own people, and I will be your God.”

So God sent plagues on Egypt. A plague is a terrible trouble that comes on a whole country. There were ten of them.

First God turned the water of the River Nile into blood. The fish died and the river stank, and nobody could drink from it.

Then came frogs. Frogs everywhere! Frogs in the houses and in the bedrooms and on the beds, frogs in the ovens and in the bread bowls.

Then came gnats, tiny biting insects, all over the people and the animals. Then swarms of flies. Then a sickness that killed the Egyptians’ cows and horses and camels. Then painful sores on the people’s skin. Then a huge hailstorm, with lightning, that smashed the crops in the fields. Then locusts, grasshoppers that ate every green thing that was left. Then darkness, a thick darkness over all Egypt for three days, so dark that people couldn’t see each other.

But here is something amazing. Where the Israelites lived, in a part of Egypt called Goshen, there were no flies, and no hail, and the animals didn’t die. And in the darkness, all the Israelites had light in their homes.

Each time a plague came, Pharaoh would say, “Pray to your God to take it away, and I will let your people go.” But each time, as soon as the trouble stopped, Pharaoh changed his mind. He made his heart hard and stubborn, and he would not let the people go.

The plagues showed that the Lord is the one true God. The Egyptians worshipped the river and the sun and many other gods. But the Lord was stronger than all of them. He ruled the river, and the animals, and the weather, and even the sun.

There was one more plague still to come. And it would be the worst of all.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 5; 7–10

Dear God, you are stronger than anyone or anything. Please keep my heart soft, so that I always listen to you and never become stubborn like Pharaoh. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Pharaoh say when Moses told him, “Let My people go”?
study_questions.answer: He said, “Who is the Lord, that I should obey Him?” and refused. Then he made the Israelites work even harder.

study_questions.question: Can you remember some of the plagues God sent on Egypt?
study_questions.answer: Water turned to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, sick animals, sores, hail, locusts and darkness. A tenth plague was still to come.

study_questions.question: Pharaoh kept promising to obey and then changing his mind. Why is it dangerous to keep saying no to God?
study_questions.answer: Every time Pharaoh said no, his heart grew harder. It’s best to listen to God straight away, while our hearts are soft.

fields.title: The Night of the Passover
fields.body_html:
“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” — Exodus 12:13

God told Moses, “I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that, he will let you go. In fact, he will drive you out.”

The last plague would be the most terrible of all. At midnight, God would pass through Egypt, and the oldest son in every family would die, from the son of Pharaoh on his throne to the son of the poorest servant girl, and even the firstborn of the animals.

But God gave His people a way to be safe.

“Every family must choose a lamb,” God said. “It must be a young male lamb, perfect, with nothing wrong with it. On the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, you must kill the lamb. Then take some of its blood and paint it on the sides and the top of the doorframe of your house.

“That night you must roast the lamb and eat it, with flat bread made without yeast, and with bitter herbs. Eat it with your sandals on your feet and your walking stick in your hand, ready to go. Eat it quickly. It is the Lord’s Passover.

“When I pass through Egypt that night, the blood on your houses will be a sign. When I see the blood, I will pass over you.”

So the Israelites did just what God said. In every Israelite home, a lamb was killed and its blood painted on the doorframe. The families stayed inside, dressed for a journey, eating their meal and waiting.

At midnight it happened, just as God had said. All over Egypt, the oldest sons died. There was loud crying everywhere in Egypt, because there wasn’t a single house where someone hadn’t died.

But in the houses with the blood on the door, everyone was safe. God passed over them.

That very night, Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron. “Get up!” he said. “Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go and worship the Lord, as you asked. Take your flocks and herds and go!”

The Egyptians begged the Israelites to hurry. The Israelites didn’t even have time to let their bread rise. They picked up their bread dough in its bowls, wrapped in their cloaks, and carried it on their shoulders. And the Egyptians gave them silver and gold and clothes as they left.

So the Israelites marched out of Egypt, about six hundred thousand men, and their wives and children too, and their flocks and herds. After 430 years in Egypt, God’s people were free!

God told them to remember that night every year, with a special meal called the Passover. Jewish families still remember it today.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jesus died on the cross at Passover time. Just as the lamb’s blood kept the families safe, Jesus’ death keeps everyone who trusts Him safe from the punishment for sin.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 11–12

Dear God, thank you that you gave the Israelites a way to be safe. Thank you for sending Jesus to be my Passover lamb. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did God tell each Israelite family to do with the lamb’s blood?
study_questions.answer: To paint it on the sides and top of the doorframe of their house, as a sign for God to pass over them.

study_questions.question: Why did the Israelites eat with their sandals on and their walking sticks in their hands?
study_questions.answer: So they would be ready to leave Egypt in a hurry, because God was about to set them free.

study_questions.question: How is Jesus like the Passover lamb?
study_questions.answer: The lamb died so the family inside would be safe. Jesus died so that everyone who trusts Him is safe from the punishment for sin. This story can raise questions about the Egyptian children, so let your child ask them, and remember together that God had warned Pharaoh many times.

On the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, you must kill the lamb. fields.title: A Path Through the Sea
fields.body_html:
“The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.” — Exodus 14:14

God led the Israelites out of Egypt. He went ahead of them in a tall pillar of cloud during the day, to show them the way. At night He was in a pillar of fire, to give them light. The pillar never left them.

God led them to camp by the edge of the Red Sea. But back in Egypt, Pharaoh changed his mind again. “What have we done?” he said. “We’ve let our slaves go!” So he got his chariot ready. He took six hundred of his best chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt, with soldiers in every one, and he chased after the Israelites.

The Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptian army thundering towards them. In front of them was the sea. Behind them were the chariots. There was nowhere to go!

They were terrified, and they cried out to Moses. “Weren’t there enough graves in Egypt, that you brought us out here to die? We told you to leave us alone! It would have been better to be slaves in Egypt than to die in the desert!”

But Moses said, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see how the Lord will save you today. The Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The Lord will fight for you. You need only to be still.”

Then the pillar of cloud moved from in front of the Israelites to behind them. It stood between them and the Egyptians, so that it was dark on the Egyptians’ side and light on the Israelites’ side. The Egyptians couldn’t come near them all night.

God told Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea.”

Moses stretched out his hand. And all that night God drove back the sea with a strong east wind. The waters split apart, and the bottom of the sea turned into dry land. The Israelites walked right through the middle of the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left!

The Egyptians chased after them, right into the middle of the sea, with all their horses and chariots. But God made the wheels of their chariots wobble, so they could hardly drive them. “Let’s get away from the Israelites!” the Egyptians shouted. “The Lord is fighting for them!”

When all the Israelites were safe on the other side, God told Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea again.” Moses did, and as morning came, the water flowed back to its place. It covered the chariots and the horsemen and Pharaoh’s whole army. Not one of them was left.

The Israelites stood on the shore and saw how great God’s power was. And they trusted God, and they trusted His servant Moses.

Then Moses and the people sang a song to God. “The Lord is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation!” Moses’ sister Miriam took a tambourine, and all the women followed her, playing tambourines and dancing. “Sing to the Lord,” Miriam sang, “for He is highly exalted. The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea!”

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 13:17–15:21

Dear God, when I am frightened and there seems to be no way out, help me to be still and trust you. Thank you that you fight for your people. Amen.

study_questions.answer: Whenever you feel trapped or frightened. Being still doesn’t mean doing nothing at all; it means trusting God instead of panicking.

fields.title: Bread from Heaven
fields.body_html:
“I will rain down bread from heaven for you.” — Exodus 16:4

The Israelites were free. But now they were walking through a hot, dry desert. There were no shops and no farms, and soon their food began to run out.

And the people began to grumble. “If only we had died in Egypt!” they said to Moses and Aaron. “There we sat around pots of meat and ate all the bread we wanted. But you have brought us out into this desert to starve us all to death!”

That wasn’t really how it had been in Egypt, was it? They had been slaves! But when people grumble, they often forget the bad things about the past and remember only the good.

God heard their grumbling. And instead of being angry, He was kind.

“I will rain down bread from heaven for you,” God told Moses. “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. On the sixth day they are to gather twice as much.”

That evening, flocks of birds called quail flew in and covered the camp. There was meat to eat!

And in the morning, when the dew had gone, there were thin white flakes all over the ground, like frost. The Israelites had never seen anything like it. “What is it?” they asked each other. In their language, that is “Man hu?” So they called it manna, which means “What is it?”

Moses said, “It is the bread the Lord has given you to eat.”

The manna was white, and it tasted like wafers made with honey. Every morning the people went out and gathered as much as they needed, one jar for each person in the family. Those who gathered a lot didn’t have too much, and those who gathered a little didn’t have too little. Everyone had just enough.

“Don’t keep any until the morning,” Moses told them. But some people didn’t listen. They kept some anyway. And by the next morning, it was full of maggots and smelled terrible!

On the sixth day, everyone gathered twice as much. “Tomorrow is a day of rest, a holy Sabbath to the Lord,” Moses said. And this time, the manna they kept overnight didn’t go bad at all. On the seventh day some people went out to gather manna anyway. But there wasn’t any. God wanted His people to rest.

God fed the Israelites with manna every single day for forty years, until they reached the land He had promised them. Every morning, there it was, a gift from heaven, just enough for that day.

God wanted His people to learn to trust Him one day at a time. They couldn’t store up food for next week. They had to trust that God would give them what they needed, each new morning.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Jesus said, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger” (John 6:35). The manna kept people alive for a day. Jesus gives life that lasts for ever.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 16

Dear God, thank you for giving me my food each day. Please help me not to grumble, but to trust you for what I need, one day at a time. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did the Israelites complain about in the desert?
study_questions.answer: They said they were going to starve, and that in Egypt they had plenty of meat and bread, forgetting they had been slaves there.

study_questions.question: What was manna like, and what did “manna” mean?
study_questions.answer: It was thin white flakes that tasted like wafers made with honey. “Manna” means “What is it?”

study_questions.question: Why do you think God gave the manna one day at a time?
study_questions.answer: So His people would learn to trust Him every day for what they needed. Jesus taught us to pray in the same way: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

fields.title: Moses’ Tired Arms
fields.body_html:
“Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side.” — Exodus 17:12

The Israelites travelled on through the desert, and they came to a place called Rephidim. But there was no water there to drink.

Once again the people grumbled. They argued with Moses. “Give us water to drink!” they said. “Why did you bring us up out of Egypt? To make us and our children and our animals die of thirst?” They were so angry that Moses thought they might throw stones at him.

Moses cried out to God. “What am I to do with these people?”

God told Moses to take some of the leaders and walk on ahead, holding the staff he had used to strike the River Nile. “I will stand there in front of you by the rock at Horeb,” God said. “Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.”

So Moses did, while the leaders watched. He struck the rock with his staff, and out gushed water! There was enough for all the people and all their animals.

Then, while they were still at Rephidim, an army came to attack them. They were called the Amalekites.

Moses said to a young man called Joshua, “Choose some men and go out and fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hands.”

So Joshua went out to fight, and Moses climbed to the top of the hill with his brother Aaron and a man called Hur.

And a strange thing happened. As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel was winning the battle. But whenever he lowered his hands, the Amalekites began to win.

Have you ever tried to hold your arms up in the air for a long time? It doesn’t take long before they start to ache and feel heavy. Moses’ arms grew so tired that he couldn’t keep them up any more.

So Aaron and Hur found a big stone and put it under Moses, and he sat on it. Then Aaron stood on one side and Hur stood on the other, and they held Moses’ hands up. They held them steady all day, until the sun went down.

And Joshua and his men won the battle.

Moses built an altar to thank God, and he gave it a name: “The Lord Is My Banner.” A banner is a flag that an army carries into battle. Moses was saying that the battle belonged to God, and God was the one who had won it.

Moses couldn’t do everything on his own. He needed Joshua to fight, and he needed Aaron and Hur to hold up his arms. God’s people need each other. Sometimes we are the ones who need help. And sometimes we are the ones who can hold up someone else’s tired arms, by helping them and praying for them.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says the rock that gave the Israelites water in the desert pointed to Jesus: “that rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Jesus gives us what we need most, just as the water came from the rock.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 17

Dear God, thank you for giving me friends and family who help me. Show me how I can help other people when they are tired or having a hard time. Amen.

study_questions.question: How did God give the people water at Rephidim?
study_questions.answer: Moses struck a rock with his staff, as God told him to, and water gushed out of it.

study_questions.question: How did Aaron and Hur help Moses during the battle?
study_questions.answer: When his arms grew tired, they sat him on a stone and held his hands up, one on each side, until the sun went down.

study_questions.question: Who could you “hold up” this week by helping them or praying for them?
study_questions.answer: Think of someone who is tired, ill, sad or finding things hard, and choose one thing you could do. You could pray for them together right now.

fields.title: Ten Good Words
fields.body_html:
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” — Exodus 20:2

Three months after they left Egypt, the Israelites came to Mount Sinai and camped at the bottom of the mountain.

God called to Moses from the mountain. “Tell the people this,” God said. “You have seen what I did to Egypt. You have seen how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself. Now, if you obey Me and keep My promise, you will be My treasured people, out of all the nations.”

The people answered, “We will do everything the Lord has said.”

On the third day, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud came down on the mountain, and a trumpet blast sounded, very loud. Everyone in the camp trembled. The whole mountain was covered in smoke, because God came down on it in fire, and the mountain shook. The trumpet grew louder and louder.

Then God spoke. He gave His people ten commandments, ten good words for them to live by.

But before He told them a single rule, God reminded them of something. “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.”

Did you notice? God rescued His people first. He didn’t say, “Keep these rules, and then I will rescue you.” He had already rescued them! The commandments were to show them how to live as His free, rescued people.

These are the ten commandments, in simple words:

  1. Do not have any other gods except Me.
  2. Do not make idols to worship.
  3. Do not misuse God’s name.
  4. Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
  5. Honour your father and your mother.
  6. Do not murder.
  7. Be faithful in marriage.
  8. Do not steal.
  9. Do not tell lies about other people.
  10. Do not covet. That means don’t long for things that belong to someone else.

The first four commandments are about loving God. The other six are about loving other people.

The people were frightened by the thunder and the smoke. “You speak to us,” they said to Moses, “and we will listen. But don’t let God speak to us, or we will die!”

“Do not be afraid,” said Moses. “God has come to test you, so that you will respect Him and not sin.”

Then Moses went up into the thick darkness on the mountain, where God was. Later, God gave Moses two flat stones with the commandments written on them, written by the finger of God Himself.

God’s commandments are good. They are like the fence around a playground, which keeps children safe from the busy road. They show us how to live well, the way God made us to live.

Looking ahead to Jesus: When someone asked Jesus which commandment was the most important, He said, “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind,” and, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37, 39). All ten commandments are about those two kinds of love. Jesus is the only one who ever kept them perfectly.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 19–20

Dear God, thank you that you rescue your people and then show us how to live. Please help me to love you with all my heart, and to love other people too. Amen.

study_questions.question: What happened on Mount Sinai when God came down?
study_questions.answer: There was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud, smoke, a very loud trumpet, and the whole mountain shook.

study_questions.question: What did God remind the people of before He gave them any commandments?
study_questions.answer: That He was the Lord their God, who had already rescued them from slavery in Egypt.

study_questions.question: Which commandment do you find hardest to keep? Why?
study_questions.answer: Talk about it honestly. Grown-ups find them hard too. None of us keeps them perfectly, which is why we need Jesus, who forgives us and helps us to change.

fields.title: The Golden Calf
fields.body_html:
“The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.” — Exodus 34:6

Moses went up Mount Sinai to be with God. He stayed there forty days and forty nights, while God told him how His people should live and worship.

Down in the camp, the people waited. And waited. And waited.

“Moses has been gone so long,” they said. “We don’t know what has happened to him.” They went to Aaron. “Come on,” they said. “Make us gods to lead us!”

Aaron should have said no. But he didn’t. “Bring me your gold earrings,” he said. The people pulled off their earrings and brought them to him. Aaron melted the gold and made it into the shape of a calf, a young bull.

And the people said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!”

Only a few weeks before, they had heard God Himself say, “Do not make idols.” They had promised, “We will do everything the Lord has said.” But now they were bowing down to a golden statue, and having a wild party around it.

Up on the mountain, God saw what they were doing. He told Moses, “Go down, because your people have turned away from Me.” God was angry, and He said He would destroy them.

But Moses prayed for the people. “Lord,” he said, “remember Your promises to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Please don’t destroy Your people.” And God listened to Moses’ prayer, and did not destroy them.

Moses went down the mountain, carrying the two stone tablets with God’s commandments on them. As he came near the camp, he heard singing, and he saw the calf and the dancing. Moses was so angry that he threw the tablets down, and they smashed to pieces at the foot of the mountain. The people had broken God’s commandments, and now the tablets were broken too.

Moses took the golden calf and burned it in the fire. He ground it into powder, scattered it on the water, and made the Israelites drink it.

“What did these people do to you,” Moses asked Aaron, “that you led them into such a great sin?”

Aaron made a silly excuse. “They gave me the gold,” he said, “and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf!”

It was a terrible day. Many people died because of their sin.

But then Moses went back up the mountain to pray for the people again. And God didn’t give up on them. He told Moses to cut two new stone tablets, and He wrote His commandments on them again.

Then God showed Moses His glory. He passed in front of Moses and called out His own name: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.” That means God is kind and full of grace. He doesn’t get angry quickly. His love is huge and it never stops.

study_questions.answer: Because Moses had been on the mountain for forty days and they got tired of waiting and didn’t know what had happened to him.

study_questions.question: What did Moses do when God was angry with the people?
study_questions.answer: He prayed for them, asking God to remember His promises, and God listened and did not destroy them.

study_questions.question: An idol is anything we love more than God. What sorts of things can become idols for people today?
study_questions.answer: Things like money, toys, screens, being popular, or winning. None of them is bad in itself, but they become idols when they matter more to us than God.

fields.title: A Tent for God
fields.body_html:
“And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them.” — Exodus 25:8

While Moses was on Mount Sinai, God told him something wonderful. God wanted to live right in the middle of His people’s camp.

“Have the people make a holy tent for Me,” God said, “so that I may live among them.” This special tent was called the tabernacle.

God gave Moses all the plans, exactly how everything should be made. The tabernacle was a tent that could be taken down and carried, because the Israelites were still travelling. It would have beautiful curtains of blue and purple and scarlet, with angels called cherubim woven into them. There would be a golden lampstand with seven lamps, and a golden table for special bread.

And at the very centre, in the most holy room of all, there would be a wooden chest covered all over with gold, called the ark of the covenant. Inside it would be the stone tablets with the commandments. On its lid were two golden cherubim, with their wings stretched out over the top.

Where would the Israelites, who had been slaves, find gold and silver and fine cloth? Do you remember? When they left Egypt, the Egyptians had given them silver and gold and clothes.

Moses asked the people to bring gifts for the tabernacle, but only if they wanted to give. And they did! Everyone whose heart moved them brought something. They brought gold brooches and earrings and rings. They brought blue and purple yarn, and fine linen, and goats’ hair, and rams’ skins dyed red. They brought wood and oil and spices and precious stones. Women who were good at spinning spun yarn, and others spun goats’ hair.

God chose a man called Bezalel to be in charge of making everything. God filled Bezalel with His Spirit and gave him wisdom and skill to work with gold and silver and bronze, to cut stones and to carve wood.

The people kept on bringing gifts, morning after morning. Soon the workers came to Moses. “The people are bringing much more than we need!” they said. So Moses sent a message all through the camp: “Don’t bring any more!” The people had to be stopped from giving, because there was already more than enough.

At last the tabernacle was finished. Everything was made just as God had said. Moses set it up in the middle of the camp.

And then a wonderful thing happened. The cloud covered the tent, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. God’s shining presence filled it so completely that even Moses couldn’t go inside.

From then on, God’s cloud stayed over the tabernacle. Whenever the cloud lifted, the Israelites packed up and followed it. And whenever it stopped, they stopped too, and camped. God was living among His people, and leading them every step of the way.

Looking ahead to Jesus: The Bible says that Jesus, God’s Son, “became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). In the language the New Testament was written in, “made His dwelling” means “pitched His tent”. When Jesus was born, God came to live among His people in a new way, not in a tent but as a real person.

Read it in your Bible: Exodus 25:1–9; 35:20–29; 36:2–7; 40:34–38

Dear God, thank you that you want to be close to your people. Thank you that Jesus came to live among us. Help me to give to you gladly, like the Israelites did. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why did God want the Israelites to make the tabernacle?
study_questions.answer: So that He could live among His people, right in the middle of their camp.

study_questions.question: What surprising thing happened when the people brought their gifts?
study_questions.answer: They brought so much more than was needed that Moses had to tell them to stop giving.

study_questions.question: The people gave gladly, because their hearts moved them. What could you give to God gladly?
study_questions.answer: Perhaps some of your money, your time, your help, or something you make. God loves it when we give because we want to, not because we have to (2 Corinthians 9:7).

fields.title: Twelve Spies
fields.body_html:
“The LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!” — Numbers 14:9

The Israelites travelled on until they came near the edge of Canaan, the land God had promised to give them.

God told Moses to send twelve men, one from each of the twelve tribes of Israel, to explore the land. “Go and see what the land is like,” Moses told them. “Are the people strong or weak? Is the soil good? Are the towns protected by walls? And bring back some of the fruit.”

So the twelve spies went. They explored the land for forty days. In one valley they cut off a bunch of grapes so enormous that two men had to carry it on a pole between them! They brought back pomegranates and figs too.

When they came back, everyone gathered to hear what they had found.

“It’s a wonderful land,” the spies said. “It really does flow with milk and honey. Look at this fruit! But the people who live there are strong, and their cities have huge walls. And we saw giants there! We felt like grasshoppers next to them.”

The people began to murmur and worry. But one of the spies, a man named Caleb, stood up and quieted them.

“We must go up and take the land,” Caleb said, “for we can certainly do it!”

But the other spies said, “No, we can’t! The people there are stronger than we are.” And they spread a frightening report all through the camp.

That night, all the people cried. They grumbled against Moses and Aaron. “If only we had died in Egypt!” they said. “Or even in this desert! Why is the Lord bringing us here to die? Let’s choose a new leader and go back to Egypt!”

Two of the spies were so upset that they tore their clothes. They were Caleb and Joshua.

“The land we explored is very, very good,” they said. “If the Lord is pleased with us, He will bring us into this land and give it to us. Only do not rebel against the Lord, and do not be afraid of the people of the land. The Lord is with us. Do not be afraid of them!”

But the people wouldn’t listen. They even picked up stones to throw at Joshua and Caleb!

Then the glory of the Lord appeared at the tabernacle. And God was very sad and angry. After everything He had done for them, the plagues and the sea and the manna and the water from the rock, they still didn’t trust Him.

So God said that the grown-ups who had refused to trust Him would never go into the land. For forty years, one year for each day the spies had explored the land, the Israelites would wander in the desert. Only Caleb and Joshua would go in. And the children, the very children the people said would die, would be the ones God would bring into the land.

Ten spies looked at the giants and thought, “They’re too big for us.” Two spies looked at the giants and thought, “They’re not too big for God.” What made the difference? Caleb and Joshua remembered how big God is.

Read it in your Bible: Numbers 13–14

Dear God, when I face something that seems as big as a giant, help me to remember that you are bigger. Help me to trust you like Caleb and Joshua did. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did the spies find in the land of Canaan?
study_questions.answer: A wonderful land with huge bunches of grapes and lots of fruit, but also strong people, cities with high walls, and giants.

study_questions.question: What was different about Caleb and Joshua?
study_questions.answer: They trusted God. They said that if God was with them, they didn’t need to be afraid, even of giants.

study_questions.question: What “giants” make you feel small or afraid? How could you remember that God is bigger?
study_questions.answer: Maybe a hard test, a bully, a fear of the dark, or a big change. We can pray about it and remember all the times God has helped His people before.

fields.title: The Snake on the Pole
fields.body_html:
“When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.” — Numbers 21:8

The Israelites wandered in the desert for many years. God still fed them with manna every morning, and He still led them with His cloud. But the people were tired and impatient, and they started grumbling again.

“Why did you bring us out of Egypt to die in the desert?” they said to God and to Moses. “There’s no bread! There’s no water! And we hate this horrible food!”

“This horrible food” was the manna, the bread from heaven that God gave them every single day.

Then God sent poisonous snakes among the people. The snakes bit them, and many of the Israelites died.

The people came to Moses. “We have sinned,” they said. “We spoke against the Lord and against you. Please pray that the Lord will take the snakes away.”

So Moses prayed for the people.

And God told Moses to do something very strange. “Make a snake and put it up on a pole,” God said. “Anyone who has been bitten can look at it, and they will live.”

So Moses made a snake out of bronze, a shiny metal, and put it up high on a pole in the middle of the camp, where everyone could see it.

Imagine you were an Israelite who had just been bitten. The poison is starting to hurt. What would you do? You could try to make medicine. You could try to suck out the poison. But God said there was only one thing that would save you: look at the snake on the pole.

It didn’t seem like much. Just a look. But it meant trusting God’s promise. And everyone who had been bitten and looked up at the bronze snake lived!

God didn’t take away all the snakes. But He gave a way to be saved from their bite, a way that was open to everyone. Nobody had to be strong, or clever, or good enough. They just had to look, and trust what God had said.

Looking ahead to Jesus: Jesus Himself talked about this story. He said, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). Jesus was lifted up on the cross. Sin is like a snake’s poison in all of us. But everyone who looks to Jesus and trusts in Him is saved.

Read it in your Bible: Numbers 21:4–9

Dear God, thank you that you made a way for people to be saved. Help me to look to Jesus and trust Him, every day. Amen.

study_questions.question: What were the Israelites grumbling about this time?
study_questions.answer: They complained that there was no bread or water, and called the manna God gave them “horrible food”.

study_questions.question: What did God tell Moses to make, and what did the people have to do to be saved?
study_questions.answer: A bronze snake on a pole. Anyone who had been bitten only had to look at it, and they would live.

study_questions.question: Jesus said He would be “lifted up” like the snake. What did He mean?
study_questions.answer: He meant He would be lifted up on the cross. Just as the Israelites only had to look to the snake, we only have to look to Jesus and trust Him to be saved from sin.

fields.title: The Donkey Who Talked
fields.body_html:
“Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth, and she said to Balaam, ‘What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?’” — Numbers 22:28

As the Israelites came near the land of Moab, the king of Moab, Balak, was terrified. “This great crowd will eat up everything around us,” he said, “like an ox eats up the grass in a field.”

Balak had an idea. There was a man called Balaam who was famous for blessing and cursing people. People said that whoever Balaam blessed was blessed, and whoever he cursed was cursed. So Balak sent messengers with money to Balaam. “Come and put a curse on these people for me,” he said.

That night God came to Balaam. “Do not go with them,” God said. “You must not curse these people, because they are blessed.”

So Balaam sent the messengers home. But King Balak sent more important messengers, with promises of even more money. This time God said Balaam could go with them, but he must only say what God told him to say.

So in the morning Balaam saddled his donkey and set off. But God was angry, because He knew what was in Balaam’s heart. So the angel of the Lord stood in the road to block his way, with a sword in his hand.

Balaam couldn’t see the angel. But his donkey could! So the donkey turned off the road into a field. Balaam hit the donkey to get her back on the road.

Then the road went between two vineyards, with a wall on each side. The angel stood there in the narrow path. The donkey saw him and squeezed against the wall, and crushed Balaam’s foot. So Balaam hit her again.

Then the angel stood in a place so narrow that there was no room to turn either way. When the donkey saw him, she just lay down under Balaam. Balaam was furious, and he beat her with his stick.

Then God opened the donkey’s mouth, and she spoke! “What have I done to you, that you have beaten me these three times?”

And Balaam was so angry he answered her! “You have made a fool of me!” he said. “If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you!”

“Am I not your own donkey,” she said, “that you have ridden all your life? Have I ever done this to you before?”

“No,” said Balaam.

Then God opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel standing in the road with his sword. Balaam bowed down with his face to the ground.

“Why have you beaten your donkey three times?” said the angel. “I came to stop you, because your path is wrong. If the donkey hadn’t turned away from me, I would have killed you by now, and let her live.”

Balaam went on to King Balak. Three times Balak took him up on a hill to look down at the Israelites and curse them. And three times Balaam opened his mouth, and blessings came out instead! “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” said Balaam.

King Balak was so cross! But nobody can curse people whom God has blessed.

Read it in your Bible: Numbers 22–24

Dear God, thank you that your blessing is stronger than anyone’s curse. Please open my eyes to see what you are doing, and help me to listen to you. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why did King Balak want Balaam to come?
study_questions.answer: He was afraid of the Israelites and wanted Balaam to put a curse on them.

study_questions.question: What did the donkey see that Balaam couldn’t see?
study_questions.answer: The angel of the Lord standing in the road with a sword, blocking the way.

study_questions.question: Every time Balaam tried to curse Israel, blessings came out instead. What does that tell us about God?
study_questions.answer: That no one can undo God’s blessing on His people. God is in charge, and He can turn even an enemy’s plans into good.

fields.title: Rahab and the Red Cord
fields.body_html:
“The LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.” — Joshua 2:11

After forty years in the desert, the Israelites were ready to go into the promised land at last. Moses had died, and God had chosen Joshua to lead the people.

Across the River Jordan was a big city with high, thick walls, called Jericho. Joshua sent two spies to look at the city secretly.

The two spies went to the house of a woman named Rahab. She was not one of God’s people, and she had not lived a good life. Her house was built right into the city wall.

But somebody saw the spies, and told the king of Jericho. The king sent men to Rahab’s house. “Bring out the men who came to your house,” they said. “They are spies!”

But Rahab had already taken the spies up onto her flat roof, and hidden them under piles of stalks of flax that she had laid out there to dry.

“Yes, the men came to me,” Rahab told the king’s men. “But I didn’t know where they were from. They left when it got dark, just before the city gate was shut. I don’t know where they went. Hurry after them, and you might catch them!”

So the king’s men rushed off towards the River Jordan to look for the spies.

Then Rahab went up onto the roof. “I know that the Lord has given you this land,” she told the spies. “Everyone here is terrified of you. “When we come into the land,” the spies told her, “tie this scarlet cord in the window you let us down from. Bring your whole family into your house. Everyone inside will be safe.”

fields.title: Crossing the Jordan
fields.body_html:
“Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.” — Joshua 1:9

After Moses died, God spoke to Joshua. “Moses my servant is dead,” God said. “Now you must lead all these people across the River Jordan into the land I am giving them. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will never leave you. Be strong and courageous! Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.”

The River Jordan was between the Israelites and the promised land. And it was harvest time, when the river was flooding over its banks. There was no bridge, and there were no boats. How could thousands and thousands of people, with their children and their animals, get across?

Joshua told the people, “Tomorrow the Lord will do amazing things among you.”

God told Joshua what to do. The priests were to carry the ark of the covenant, the golden chest from the tabernacle, and walk ahead of the people, right into the river.

So the next day, the people packed up their tents and set off, with the priests carrying the ark in front. The river was deep and fast. But as soon as the priests’ feet touched the edge of the water, the river stopped flowing! The water piled up far away upstream, at a town called Adam. And the riverbed in front of them was dry.

The priests carrying the ark walked into the middle of the river and stood there on dry ground. And the whole nation of Israel walked across, right past them, on dry ground.

It was just like the Red Sea, forty years before! The children who had grown up in the desert had heard their parents tell that story. Now they saw God do it again for them.

When everyone had crossed, God told Joshua, “Choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Tell them to take twelve stones from the middle of the river, from right where the priests are standing.”

So the twelve men each picked up a big stone from the riverbed, carried it on his shoulder, and brought it to the place where they camped that night.

When the priests carrying the ark came up out of the river, and their feet touched dry land, the water came rushing back and flooded over its banks again, just as before.

Joshua set up the twelve stones in a pile. “In the future,” he said, “your children will ask you, ‘What do these stones mean?’ Then you can tell them, ‘The River Jordan stopped flowing in front of the ark of the Lord.’ These stones will help the people of Israel remember for ever.”

God did this, Joshua said, “so that all the people of the earth may know that the hand of the Lord is mighty, and so that you may always fear the Lord your God.”

Read it in your Bible: Joshua 1:1–9; 3–4

Dear God, thank you that you are with me wherever I go. Help me to be strong and brave, and to remember all the good things you have done. Amen.

study_questions.question: What happened when the priests’ feet touched the water of the River Jordan?
study_questions.answer: The river stopped flowing and piled up far upstream, and the riverbed became dry so everyone could cross.

study_questions.question: Why did Joshua set up twelve stones from the river?
study_questions.answer: So that when children asked, “What do these stones mean?”, their parents could tell them how God stopped the river.

study_questions.question: What are some things God has done for your family that you could remember and tell others about?
study_questions.answer: Think of answers to prayer, times God helped or kept you safe, or how people in your family came to know Him. You could even write them down or draw them.

fields.title: The Walls of Jericho
fields.body_html:
“The people gave a great shout, and the wall collapsed.” — Joshua 6:20

The city of Jericho was shut up tight. Its gates were locked and barred, and its walls were high and strong. Nobody went out and nobody came in, because the people of Jericho were afraid of the Israelites.

How could the Israelites ever get inside? They didn’t have ladders tall enough, or machines to knock down walls.

But God told Joshua, “See, I have given Jericho into your hands.” And God gave him a very strange battle plan.

“March around the city once a day for six days, with all your soldiers,” God said. “Seven priests are to carry trumpets made of rams’ horns in front of the ark. On the seventh day, march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the trumpets. When you hear a long blast on the trumpets, all the people must give a loud shout. Then the wall of the city will fall down flat.”

It must have sounded like a very odd way to fight a battle! But Joshua told the people exactly what God had said.

So on the first day, the soldiers marched around the city, with the priests blowing their trumpets and carrying the ark. “Don’t shout,” Joshua told the people. “Don’t say a word until the day I tell you to shout.” So round they went, once, in silence except for the trumpets. Then they went back to their camp.

On the second day, they did the same. And the third day, and the fourth, and the fifth, and the sixth. Can you imagine the people of Jericho, peeping over the walls, wondering what was going on?

On the seventh day, they got up at dawn and marched around the city. Once, twice, three times, four, five, six, seven times! On the seventh time round, the priests blew a long blast on their trumpets.

“Shout!” said Joshua. “For the Lord has given you the city!”

The people gave a great shout. And the walls of Jericho fell down flat! Every soldier charged straight into the city and took it.

Jericho was a wicked city, and God had said it would be destroyed. Its people died in the battle. But there was one house that was kept safe: the house with the red cord hanging from the window. Joshua sent the two spies to Rahab’s house, and they brought out Rahab and her whole family, just as they had promised. Rahab trusted God, and God saved her and everyone who came into her house.

The Israelites didn’t win the battle of Jericho by being strong, or clever, or by having better weapons. They won by trusting God and doing what He said, even when it seemed strange.

Read it in your Bible: Joshua 6

Dear God, thank you that nothing is too strong for you. Help me to obey you even when I don’t understand why, and to trust you to keep your promises. Amen.

study_questions.question: What was God’s plan for taking Jericho?
study_questions.answer: To march around the city once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day, with the priests blowing trumpets, and then everyone shouting.

study_questions.question: Who was kept safe when Jericho fell, and why?
study_questions.answer: Rahab and her whole family, because she had trusted God and hidden the spies, and they kept their promise to her.

study_questions.question: The Israelites obeyed God even though His plan seemed strange. Why do you think they did?
study_questions.answer: They had seen God do amazing things before, like the Red Sea and the Jordan, so they trusted Him. The more we remember what God has done, the easier it is to trust Him.

fields.title: Deborah and the Rainstorm
fields.body_html:
“Has not the LORD gone before you?” — Judges 4:14

After Joshua died, the Israelites lived in the promised land. But they kept forgetting God. They worshipped the false gods of the people around them. And every time they turned away from God, trouble came.

This time the trouble was a king called Jabin, from the land of Canaan. The commander of his army was a man named Sisera, and Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots. For twenty years he was cruel to the Israelites. At last they cried out to God for help.

In those days, God’s people were led by a woman named Deborah. She was a prophetess, which means God spoke to her and through her. Deborah used to sit under a palm tree in the hill country, and the Israelites came to her to settle their quarrels and to hear what God said.

Deborah sent for a man named Barak. “The Lord, the God of Israel, commands you,” she told him. “Take ten thousand men and go to Mount Tabor. God will lead Sisera and his chariots to the river Kishon, and He will give him into your hands.”

But Barak said, “If you go with me, I will go. But if you don’t go with me, I won’t go.”

“All right, I will go with you,” said Deborah. “But because of the way you are doing this, you won’t get the honour. The Lord will hand Sisera over to a woman.”

So Deborah went with Barak, and ten thousand men followed them up Mount Tabor.

When Sisera heard about it, he gathered all his nine hundred iron chariots and his whole army, and brought them to the river Kishon, below the mountain.

Then Deborah said to Barak, “Go! This is the day the Lord has given Sisera into your hands. Has not the Lord gone ahead of you?”

So Barak charged down the mountain with his ten thousand men. And God threw Sisera and all his chariots and his army into a panic. The song that Deborah sang afterwards tells us that the sky poured with rain and the river Kishon flooded. Those heavy iron chariots got stuck in the mud and swept away! Sisera jumped down from his chariot and ran away on foot.

Sisera ran until he came to the tent of a woman named Jael. Jael invited him in, gave him milk to drink, and covered him with a blanket. Sisera was so tired that he fell fast asleep. And while he slept, brave Jael made sure that Sisera would never trouble God’s people again.

So Deborah’s words came true. The honour for defeating Sisera went to a woman.

Then Deborah and Barak sang a song of praise to God. “May all who love You shine like the sun at its brightest!” they sang. And there was peace in the land for forty years.

Read it in your Bible: Judges 4–5

Dear God, thank you that you go ahead of your people. Thank you for brave women like Deborah and Jael. Help me to be brave and to follow you. Amen.

study_questions.question: Who was Deborah, and what did she do?
study_questions.answer: She was a prophetess and a leader of Israel. She sat under a palm tree and helped people settle quarrels, and she told Barak what God wanted him to do.

study_questions.question: How did God defeat Sisera’s nine hundred iron chariots?
study_questions.answer: He sent heavy rain, the river flooded, and the chariots got stuck and were swept away, so Sisera ran away on foot.

study_questions.question: Deborah said, “Has not the Lord gone ahead of you?” How does it help to know that God goes ahead of us?
study_questions.answer: We never go anywhere that God hasn’t already been. Whatever is coming, like a new school or a hard day, He is already there.

fields.title: Gideon’s Small Army
fields.body_html:
“The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” — Judges 6:12

Once again the Israelites forgot God and did wrong. So God let a people called the Midianites rule over them. Every year, when the Israelites had planted their crops, the Midianites came swarming in like locusts, with their camels, and took everything. The Israelites had to hide in caves in the mountains.

One day a young man called Gideon was threshing wheat. Normally people threshed wheat out in the open, where the wind could blow away the husks. But Gideon was hiding in a winepress, a pit in the ground, so that the Midianites wouldn’t see him.

Then the angel of the Lord appeared to him. “The Lord is with you, mighty warrior!” he said.

Gideon must have looked around to see who he was talking to! He certainly didn’t feel like a mighty warrior. “If the Lord is with us,” Gideon said, “why has all this happened to us?”

“Go in the strength you have,” said the Lord, “and save Israel from the Midianites. Am I not sending you?”

“But how can I save Israel?” said Gideon. “My family is the weakest in our whole tribe, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.”

“I will be with you,” the Lord said.

Gideon still wasn’t sure. So he asked God for a sign. “I will put a woolly fleece on the threshing floor,” he said. “If there is dew on the fleece in the morning, but the ground all around it is dry, then I will know You will save Israel through me.” The next morning, the fleece was so wet he wrung out a whole bowl of water! But the ground was dry.

Then Gideon asked again. “Don’t be angry with me. This time, let the fleece be dry, and the ground covered with dew.” And God did that too!

So Gideon gathered an army. Thirty-two thousand men came. But God said, “You have too many men. If you win, Israel will boast, ‘We saved ourselves.’”

So Gideon told everyone who was afraid to go home. Twenty-two thousand men went home! Ten thousand were left.

“There are still too many,” God said. He told Gideon to take the men down to the water to drink. Most of them knelt down to drink. But three hundred men scooped up the water in their hands and lapped it. “With these three hundred men I will save you,” said God.

Three hundred men, against an army as many as locusts!

In the middle of the night, Gideon gave each man a trumpet and an empty clay jar with a burning torch hidden inside it. They crept to the edge of the enemy camp and spread out all around it. Then Gideon blew his trumpet. All three hundred men blew their trumpets and smashed their jars, so that the torches blazed out in the dark. And they shouted, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”

The Midianites woke up to trumpets and crashing and fire and shouting all around them. They panicked! In the confusion, they turned on each other, and then ran away.

God won the battle, with just three hundred men. Everyone knew it was God, not Gideon, who had saved them.

Read it in your Bible: Judges 6–7

Dear God, when I feel small and weak, remind me that you are with me. Thank you that you can do great things through people who seem unimportant. Amen.

study_questions.question: What was Gideon doing when the angel came, and what did the angel call him?
study_questions.answer: He was secretly threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding from the Midianites. The angel called him “mighty warrior”.

study_questions.question: Why did God make Gideon’s army so small?
study_questions.answer: So that the Israelites wouldn’t boast that they had saved themselves, and everyone would know that God had won the battle.

study_questions.question: Gideon felt weak and small, but God chose him. Do you ever feel too small to do anything for God?
study_questions.answer: God loves to use people who feel small, because then everyone can see that it’s His power. What matters is that God is with you.

fields.body_html:
“O Lord GOD, please remember me.” — Judges 16:28

The Israelites did wrong again, and this time God let a people called the Philistines rule over them for forty years.

There was a man named Manoah and his wife, who had no children. One day the angel of the Lord came to Manoah’s wife. “You are going to have a son,” he said. “No razor must ever touch his head. He will be set apart for God from the day he is born, and he will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines.”

The boy was born, and they called him Samson. As he grew up, God blessed him. His hair grew long, and God made him amazingly strong. Once, when a young lion came roaring at him, the Spirit of the Lord came on Samson and he tore it apart with his bare hands! Samson fought the Philistines again and again, all by himself.

But Samson didn’t always follow God. He did what he wanted, and he often made foolish choices.

Samson fell in love with a woman called Delilah. The rulers of the Philistines went to Delilah. “Find out the secret of his great strength,” they said, “and we will each give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”

So Delilah asked Samson, “Tell me the secret of your great strength.”

Samson teased her. “If anyone ties me up with seven new bowstrings, I’ll be as weak as anyone else.” So while he slept she tied him up with bowstrings, and shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” But he snapped the bowstrings like thread.

She asked again, and he said, “New ropes.” But he snapped those too. The third time, he said, “Weave my hair into your loom.” But he pulled it all out.

“How can you say you love me,” Delilah said, “when you won’t tell me your secret?” She nagged him day after day, until he was sick of it. At last Samson told her everything. “No razor has ever touched my head,” he said. “If my head is shaved, my strength will leave me.”

So Delilah let him fall asleep with his head on her knees, and she called a man to shave off his hair. “Samson, the Philistines are here!” she shouted.

Samson woke up and thought, “I’ll get free like before.” But he didn’t know that the Lord had left him.

The Philistines grabbed him. They blinded him and took him away to prison, and made him grind grain like an animal. But in prison, his hair began to grow again.

One day the Philistines held a great party in the temple of their god, Dagon. “Our god has given us Samson!” they cheered. “Bring him out to entertain us!”

So they brought Samson out, and stood him between the pillars that held up the temple. The temple was packed with thousands of people.

Then Samson prayed. “O Lord God, please remember me. Make me strong just once more.”

Samson put his hands on the two middle pillars, one on each side, and pushed with all his might. The pillars gave way, and the whole temple came crashing down on everyone inside, Samson too. In his death, Samson defeated more Philistines than in all his life.

Samson made many mistakes. But at the very end, when he had nothing left, he called out to God, and God heard him.

Read it in your Bible: Judges 13; 16

Dear God, thank you that my strength comes from you. Help me to make wise choices. And thank you that even when I mess things up, I can always call out to you. Amen.

study_questions.question: Why was Samson never meant to cut his hair?
study_questions.answer: Because he had been set apart for God from the day he was born, and his long hair was the sign of that promise.

study_questions.question: How did the Philistines finally capture Samson?
study_questions.answer: Delilah nagged him until he told her his secret, then had his head shaved while he slept, and his strength left him because God had left him.

study_questions.question: Samson made lots of foolish choices, but at the end he prayed and God heard him. What does that teach us?
study_questions.answer: It’s always better to follow God from the start. But it’s never too late to call out to Him, and He hears us even after we’ve made a mess of things.

fields.title: Ruth Stays with Naomi
fields.body_html:
“Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” — Ruth 1:16

In the days when judges ruled Israel, there was a famine in the land. There wasn’t enough food in Bethlehem. So a man from Bethlehem took his wife, Naomi, and their two sons, and went to live in the country of Moab.

While they were there, Naomi’s husband died. Her two sons married women from Moab, called Orpah and Ruth. But about ten years later, both of the sons died too. Naomi was left all alone in a foreign country, with no husband and no sons.

Then Naomi heard that God had given His people food again in Israel. So she set off home to Bethlehem, and her two daughters-in-law went with her.

On the way, Naomi stopped. “Go back to your own mothers’ homes,” she told them. “May the Lord be kind to you, as you have been kind to me and to my sons.” She kissed them goodbye, and they all cried.

Orpah kissed Naomi and went back home. But Ruth held on to her.

“Look,” said Naomi, “your sister-in-law is going back to her people and her gods. Go back with her.”

But Ruth said, “Don’t ask me to leave you. Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.”

Ruth was choosing to leave her own country and everything she knew. She was choosing to look after Naomi. And she was choosing to follow the God of Israel.

So the two women came to Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was excited. “Can this be Naomi?” the women said.

“Don’t call me Naomi,” she said. Naomi means “pleasant”. “Call me Mara,” she said, which means “bitter”. “I went away full, but the Lord has brought me back empty.”

It was the start of the barley harvest. Ruth and Naomi had nothing to eat. But God’s law said that when farmers harvested their fields, they must leave some grain behind for poor people and foreigners to pick up. This was called gleaning.

So Ruth went out to glean. And she happened to go to a field that belonged to a man named Boaz, who was a relative of Naomi’s husband.

Boaz came from Bethlehem to see his workers. “The Lord be with you!” he called to them. “The Lord bless you!” they called back.

Boaz noticed Ruth. “Who is that young woman?” he asked.

“She’s the one from Moab who came back with Naomi,” said his foreman. “She has been working hard all day.”

Boaz went to Ruth. “Stay in my field,” he said kindly. “Don’t go anywhere else. Stay with my servant girls, and when you’re thirsty, drink from the water jars.” He had heard all about how Ruth had left her own family to look after Naomi. “May the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge, reward you richly,” he said.

At lunchtime Boaz gave Ruth bread and roasted grain, so much that she had some left over. And he quietly told his workers, “Pull out some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to pick up.”

When Ruth came home that evening with a huge bundle of barley, Naomi was amazed. “Where did you glean today?” she asked. “Bless the man who noticed you!”

“His name is Boaz,” said Ruth.

“The Lord bless him!” said Naomi. “The Lord has not stopped being kind to us! That man is one of our close relatives.”

Read it in your Bible: Ruth 1–2

Dear God, thank you that you take care of people who are lonely and sad. Help me to be loyal and kind, like Ruth and like Boaz. Amen.

study_questions.question: What did Ruth say to Naomi when Naomi told her to go back home?
study_questions.answer: “Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.”

study_questions.question: How was Boaz kind to Ruth?
study_questions.answer: He let her glean in his field, told her to stay safe with his servant girls, gave her water and food, and told his workers to leave extra grain for her.

study_questions.question: Ruth stayed with Naomi when it would have been easier to leave. Who could you be loyal and kind to?
study_questions.answer: Perhaps a friend who is having a hard time, a grandparent, or someone new and lonely. Being faithful to people, even when it’s hard, is one way we show God’s love.
